title: Stay in the shade
hookLine: out of the sun, into the shade, and back out again
carry: joy is the self's own, not the thing's

lines: INTO THE SHADE, AND OUT AGAIN.
cards: Midday, a hot road, no wind. A traveler steps under a tree and the relief is instant. A few minutes later, something across the road catches the eye, and the traveler walks back out into the glare to get it.
Then back to the shade. Then out again. Ramana Maharshi draws that scene in Who Am I?, near the end, and he uses it to answer the question the text opened with: where is happiness?

teach.b: Remember how the text began: everyone wants to be happy. Here, Ramana says where that happiness is. Not in things.
When we get something we wanted, we feel happy, and we credit the thing. But what really happened, in his account, is that the wanting stopped for a moment.

The mind went quiet and turned back toward the self, and the happiness we felt was the self's own. Vedanta's name for the self is sat-chit-ananda: being, awareness, bliss. Ramana's shade is that ananda.
Then the next want shows up, and we walk back into the sun. The one who knows this, he says, stays in the shade. Close by, a line for anyone who feels too far gone.
Even someone who has done great wrong, Ramana says, shouldn't sit weeping, I'm a sinner, how can I be saved?
Drop that thought, he says, and get on with the inquiry. The heavy story about yourself is one more thought. Now look back at this week.
Narendra asking, have you seen God? A monkey, and the one watching it. A lake, and the atman at the bottom.
A boy lying down as if dead. The stick that burns at the end. An elephant given a chain.

teach.h: THE WISE ONE STAYS IN THE SHADE.
teach.b: And the shade. Two teachers, and in both their accounts one claim underneath: what the seeker is looking for was there before the looking started.

how: Readers of Who Am I? return to it as a daily text; at Ramana's ashram in Tiruvannamalai, visitors sit in silence in the hall where he lived and walk around the hill of Arunachala.

o: a saint who said a great sinner can never be saved
a teacher who said joy comes from getting what you want
the sage who said happiness is the self's own, not in things

games.q: a week of the mind — tap the pairs.

s: Ramana says happiness comes from the things we get
he says when a want is met the mind goes quiet, and the happiness felt is the self's own.
he tells someone who feels like a great sinner to drop that thought and keep inquiring
the heavy story about yourself is one more thought, given the same question.
the person in the shade picture keeps walking back into the sun
that's the ordinary mind, chasing wants; the wise one, Ramana says, stays in the shade.

games.q: you've done real wrong, and you feel too far gone for any of this. what does Ramana say?
o: you must first make up for all of it.
drop the thought 'I'm a sinner' and get on with the inquiry.
this path isn't for people like you.
games.why: in Who Am I?, he says not to sit weeping 'how can I be saved?', but to give up the thought 'I am a sinner' and keep at the inquiry.

practice: Recall one small happiness from this week, a meal, a message, a moment of quiet, and notice how, just then, the wanting paused; see if you can find that pause again without the thing, and rest in the shade.
When a want pulls you back into the sun, or a heavy thought about yourself arrives, ask whose it is. If you pray, you can let the resting be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said happiness isn't in things but is the self's own, and that the wise one stays in the shade.

orig.note: Tamil, in Tamil script: Nan Yar, 'who am I?', the name of Ramana's text in the language he wrote it in.

carryVoice: Your line: joy is the self's own, not the thing's. Tomorrow, a different kind of teacher: Aurobindo. Day nine hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.
